The NYISO defines a backstop cost allocation method based on load ratio share for public policy projects but allows for alternative methods to be developed to fit each transmission project need. Alternative cost allocation methods can be proposed by the NYPSC or the entity selected by the NYISO to develop the project with NYPSC approval. For the AC Transmission Needs project, the NYPSC recommended an alternative cost allocation scheme whereby 75% of costs would be allocated to economic beneficiaries, measured as reductions in anticipated congestion over a 10- year period, and 25% would be based on load ratio share based on forecasted summer peak demand (State of New York Public Service Commission Order Finding Transmission Needs Driven by Public Policy Requirements 2015). This alternative was adopted by the NYISO because it allows for more granular cost allocation to load downstate, which bears the largest cost responsibility. 3.2.3 SPP Priority Projects SPP applies a unique cost allocation approach to its “Priority Projects” and “Integrated Transmission Plan” (ITP) projects based on a voltage threshold to allocate costs on a load ratio share basis between regions and local zones, also known as the Highway/Byway method. The SPP Priority Projects consisted of five 345-kV single-circuit and double-circuit transmission lines in Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Nebraska, and Missouri (Figure 7). These projects were identified in 2009 by the Synergistic Planning Project Team (SPPT) to relieve congestion across the network, integrate new generation resources, and connect the east and west portions of SPP’s footprint (SPP 2009). The SPPT estimated the Priority Projects would provide $3.7 billion in benefits across the region through a range of quantified benefits, including production cost savings, reduced losses, deferred capacity investments, and improved reliability (SPP 2010b). After approval by the SPP Board of Directors in 2010, all Priority Projects were completed in 2017 (SPP 2025a). Figure 7. SPP Priority Projects. Costs for SPP’s Priority Projects and subsequent ITPs are allocated through the region’s unique Highway/Byway method. The philosophy behind this method is that higher-voltage lines provide benefits across the entire region, whereas lower-voltage lines provide more localized benefits. As a result, costs for higher-voltage lines should be borne by the entire region, and those for lower- voltage lines should be paid by the local zones where the project is located. The SPP’s Regional State Committee (RSC) developed a Highway/Byway approach to replace SPP’s three existing methods at the time, which included separate rates for zonal projects and regional projects, a load ratio share rate for Balance Portfolio projects, and a new yet-to-be-determined rate for extra- high-voltage projects.
